title: Content analysis of bone sarcoma-related hashtags on instagram: Themes, engagement patterns, and public health implications
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 1201 bone sarcoma-related Instagram posts, one of whose stated aims was 'to assess the prevalence of health misinformation'. Reports the share of posts classified as misinformation (5.7%, 68/1201) against an explicit three-tier falsity framework judged against peer-reviewed literature. This is a CONTENT share with a stated denominator.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language Instagram posts worldwide (authors based in Turkiye)
estimates.measure_type: % of bone sarcoma-related Instagram posts classified as misinformation (clearly false, or misleading/unverified)
estimates.denominator: 1201 unique publicly accessible, English-language, bone sarcoma-related Instagram posts obtained by stratified random sampling (weighted by hashtag volume) across ten predefined bone sarcoma hashtags, July 2025-January 2026
estimates.definition: A post counted in the numerator if coded tier (a) 'clearly false' -- direct factual errors contradicted by peer-reviewed literature (e.g. claims that specific supplements cure bone sarcoma) -- or tier (b) 'misleading or unverified' -- unsubstantiated assertions lacking any supporting evidence but not directly refuted. Tier (c) 'oversimplified' (accurate information presented without essential clinical qualification) was NOT counted as misinformation.
estimates.misinfo_def: "misinformation was operationalised using a three-tier framework: (a) clearly false, comprising direct factual errors contradicted by peer-reviewed literature...; (b) misleading or unverified, comprising unsubstantiated assertions lacking any supporting evidence but not directly refuted; and (c) oversimplified... For analytical purposes, only tiers (a) and (b) were classified as Misinformation"
estimates.source_quote: Misinformation was identified in 5.7% of posts.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (Results); the count appears in Results, section 3, p. 2 ("Misinformation wasidentified in 68 posts (5.7%), concentrated within Medical/Clinical Information and Commercial/Promotional categories" -- note the missing space is an OCR artefact in the source text) and in Table 4 ("Misinformation 68") and Methods ("Misinformation (n = 68)")
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent coders with backgrounds in health communication and clinical oncology coded all 1201 posts using a structured manual with operational definitions, decision trees and annotated examples; overall Cohen's kappa on a random 20% subsample (n=240) = 0.87 (95% CI 0.83-0.91); discrepancies resolved by consensus. Clinical accuracy was additionally evaluated by two orthopaedic oncology specialists against AAOS guidelines, contemporary systematic reviews and a factual-error criterion, with discrepancies resolved in a consensus meeting; the authors note criterion-level inter-rater agreement was not formally quantified.
estimates.moderator_quote: A cross-sectional content analysis was conducted on publicly accessible Instagram posts published between July 1, 2025 and January 31, 2026. Ten hashtags were selected via a two-phase process... A stratified random sampling strategy—weighted by hashtag volume—yielded 1201 unique posts meeting inclusion criteria: publicly accessible, English-language, bone sarcoma-related, and within the study period.
estimates.notes: Judgement calls for an adjudicator. (a) Under-count by design: misinformation is one of NINE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE thematic categories, so a post only counts if misinformation was its dominant theme; the authors flag this themselves ('the mutually exclusive single-category coding scheme prevents the capture of content that spans multiple themes... which may underestimate the co-occurrence of misinformation within otherwise legitimate content'). (b) STRUCTURAL INCONSISTENCY IN THE PAPER: Table 2 lists only eight categories and they sum exactly to 1201 (341+274+186+142+101+87+42+28), with NO Misinformation row -- yet 68 posts are said to be misinformation and Table 4 treats Misinformation (n=68) as a category distinct from Medical/Clinical Information (n=101). Table 2's 'Misinfo*' column instead reads as a within-category flag (Medical/Clinical Info 'Partial', Commercial/Promotional 'Yes'). So the paper is self-contradictory about whether misinformation is a category or a flag. The value 5.7% and the denominator 1201 are stated consistently in the Abstract, Results and Table 2, so the row itself stands; the composition is what is unclear. (c) Data collection straddles two calendar years (Jul 2025-Jan 2026); year coded as 2025, the start and the bulk of the window.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, with reasons: (1) QAMAI information-quality scores are reported only as MEANS (Medical/Clinical Information 15.8 +/- 3.2; Misinformation posts 9.2 +/- 2.6; overall 13.1 +/- 4.5, on a 5-25 composite), with a stated low-quality threshold of <=15 but NO share of posts falling below it. Scale means with no derivable share, so no QUALITY row. (2) Thematic distribution (patient narrative 28.4%, motivational 22.8%, awareness 15.5%, caregiver 11.8%, medical/clinical 8.4%, fundraising 7.3%, research 3.5%, commercial 2.3%) is topic composition, not misinformation prevalence. (3) Account-type distribution and engagement rates (Table 3) and median likes/comments/shares (Table 2) are not veracity measures. (4) Kolade et al.'s 'mean misinformation index of 2.11/5.00' and the '16.1% vs 83.9%' engagement split are figures the paper cites from elsewhere -- excluded by R8. (5) No within-misinformation falsity split (tier a vs tier b) is reported, so no stricter definition variant is available.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of publicly accessible Instagram posts, 1 July 2025 - 31 January 2026. Sampling frame: ten bone sarcoma hashtags chosen by a two-phase process (MeSH-derived plus lay seed list, then snowball sampling of co-occurring hashtags exceeding 5000 posts); stratified random sampling weighted by hashtag volume; inclusion required publicly accessible, English-language, bone sarcoma-related and in-window; de-duplication at sampling. n=1201 posts. Coding: nine mutually exclusive categories developed a priori and refined on 100 pilot posts excluded from the final sample; two independent coders (health communication and clinical oncology backgrounds) coded all posts; Cohen's kappa on a random 20% subsample (n=240) = 0.87 (95% CI 0.83-0.91); consensus resolution. Misinformation operationalised on a three-tier framework with only tiers (a) clearly false and (b) misleading/unverified counted. Clinical accuracy separately rated by two orthopaedic oncology specialists against AAOS guidelines, systematic reviews and factual accuracy (met / partially met / not met), consensus for discrepancies, criterion-level agreement not quantified. QAMAI quality scoring applied only to the Medical/Clinical Information and Misinformation categories (n=169), ICC 0.84 overall. Analysis in SPSS 28 with Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn post-hoc. No IRB approval (public data). Authors' limitations include English-only sampling bias, ten-hashtag coverage limits, single-category coding under-capturing co-occurring misinformation, and unmeasured near-duplicate reposting.

For analytical purposes, only tiers (a) and (b) were classified as Misinformation
